clue.text: Activity for boys, namely Latin trip

blocks.note: sc. abbreviates scilicet, the Latin word for namely
an outing is a short trip

explanation.surface: A youth leader describes a boys' club activity: a trip to study Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scout movement has long organised camping, badges and outdoor pursuits mainly for boys.

clue.text: Patient packing royal couple’s expensive clothing?

indicators.note: a case packing something holds it inside, so the royal letters go within the patient

blocks.note: a doctor's patient is a case
two royal abbreviations side by side: HM (His or Her Majesty) and ER (Elizabeth Regina)

explanation.surface: A hospital patient is somehow carrying the royal couple's luxurious wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal pair sits between the S and E of the patient, giving CAS-HMER-E.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is fine, costly goat wool used for luxury jumpers and scarves; the question mark flags it as one example of pricey garments.

clue.text: Very bitter officer decorated coats

indicators.note: a coating wraps around what it covers, so the decorated word surrounds the officer

blocks.note: a cake decorated with icing is iced
Col is the abbreviation for colonel

explanation.surface: A sour, resentful officer who has just been given a medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decorated' looks like a medal for the officer, but it is a cake word: icing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitter weather is extremely cold, so very bitter means frozen through.

clue.text: Kind of red bird seen by Celt

blocks.note: the tit is a small songbird
Ian is the Scottish form of John, so stands for a Celt

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher from the Celtic fringe spots a red-feathered bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Titian is the auburn, reddish-gold hair colour named after the Venetian painter who favoured it.

clue.text: Two Americans receiving a lot of support? You can count on it

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter goes
the two Americans take in another word between them, as if receiving a guest

blocks.note: counts the American pieces: two separate abbreviations are wanted
A is a standard abbreviation for American
to back someone is to support them
US, the United States, is the second American

explanation.surface: Two Americans get plenty of backing, and you can rely on that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two' tells you to find two separate American abbreviations, A and US, which become the bookends.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of beads used for calculating, quite literally a thing you count on.

clue.text: Party member with hesitation about Conservative, one keen on standing

indicators.note: about here means alongside, so the member and hesitation are set right next to the Conservative

blocks.note: a social is an informal party
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
an arm or leg is a member of the body
er is the sound of hesitating

explanation.surface: A hesitant party member wavers over the Conservatives, ready to stand for election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' suggests standing for office; it means social status.
explanation.definitionFit: A social climber is eager to raise their status in society, so is keen on improving their standing.

clue.text: Needing area for circle, foolishly I soon miscount pi

indicators.note: needing area for circle tells you one letter must be swapped in place of another
doing something foolishly means doing it wrongly, so the letters come out in a muddled order

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area
a circle is shaped like the letter O
the letters as written

explanation.surface: A maths pupil frets that needing the area of a circle, they will foolishly miscount pi.
explanation.walkthrough: Pi looks like the number 3.14 from the circle's area formula; it is the slang short form of pious. One O of the fodder becomes A before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Pi is informal British slang for pious, and sanctimonious means making a show of piety.

clue.text: Frequently slip after shower, we hear, in dark period

indicators.note: we hear signals that the shower word is only to be heard, then written another way

blocks.note: a shower is rain, which is said the same as the word for a monarch's rule
oft is an old word for often
a slip is a mistake

explanation.surface: Someone keeps slipping over after a shower during a gloomy spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the shower piece first, ahead of the frequently and slip pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Reign of Terror was the bloody phase of the French Revolution in 1793-94, a notoriously grim era.

clue.text: Ample figure giving a twirl? I’m horrified!

indicators.note: a twirl spins something round, so the figure is turned to face the other way

blocks.note: one is a number, or figure
ugh is a cry of disgust

explanation.surface: Someone twirls to show off an ample figure and an onlooker recoils in horror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ample figure' reads as a curvy body, but 'Ample' is the definition and 'figure' a number.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means sufficient, and enough means as much as is needed.

clue.text: Middle part of three inches, perhaps, is so long

indicators.note: the middle part of something is what remains when both ends are trimmed off

blocks.note: the unit word written out three times in a row

explanation.surface: Three inches is the middle part of something long, perhaps a ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: Write INCH three times and drop IN from the front and CH from the back. 'Perhaps' warns that the inches are to be taken literally as words.
explanation.definitionFit: Chin-chin is an old-fashioned informal farewell or toast, so it can mean goodbye, like so long.

clue.text: Beastly noise from pet shaking tail

indicators.note: shaking off a tail means losing the final letter

blocks.note: a pet is a fit of sulking, a bad mood

explanation.surface: A pet animal makes a dreadful racket while wagging its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: Pet is the noun for a sulk, as in 'in a pet', not a domestic animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A moo is the sound a cow makes, a noise from a beast.

clue.text: Vacuous skiffle covers get wasted for band

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so only the outside letters of the word stay
a cover goes around what it hides, so the emptied word wraps the other piece

blocks.note: the first and last letters of skiffle
to trip is to be high on drugs

explanation.surface: A shallow skiffle band covers songs and gets drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' looks like a band playing cover versions; it is the container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripe is a long narrow strip of colour, which is a band.

clue.text: Advance across rolling sand in promontory

indicators.note: rolling things tumble over, so the letters land in a new order
spread across something means stretched over it on both sides, enclosing it

blocks.note: to advance money is to lend it
the letters of sand rearranged

explanation.surface: Walkers press on across rolling dunes on a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Land's End is the headland at the far south-western tip of Cornwall, England's best-known promontory.

clue.text: Reporter’s expected au pair

indicators.note: a reporter speaks the words, so we go by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: expected is due, and the French au is said oh

explanation.surface: A journalist's long-awaited au pair is about to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Au pair' looks like a single phrase for a live-in helper, but it splits: au supplies a sound, pair is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A duo is a set of two people or things, which is a pair.

clue.text: More pleased with number one runner losing pound

indicators.note: losing something means it goes missing, so a letter drops out

blocks.note: a gun-runner or rum-runner is a smuggler
L, from Latin libra, stands for a pound

explanation.surface: A winning runner, delighted with first place, has lost a pound of weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one' looks like first place in a race; here it means oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Smug means self-satisfied, and number one is slang for oneself, so smugger is more pleased with yourself.

clue.text: Suffering a reversal, cricket side come together

indicators.note: suffering a reversal means being turned back, so the side is read from right to left

blocks.note: in cricket the leg side is the half of the field behind the batsman's legs

explanation.surface: A cricket team that has lost a match needs to rally and bond.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket has two sides of the field, off and leg; the leg side is the one the batter stands facing away from.
explanation.definitionFit: When a team gels, its members come together and start working well as a unit.

clue.text: Praise grand vehicle having provided for queen

indicators.note: having one thing for another means it stands in place of it, a straight swap

blocks.note: G is short for grand, a thousand
a lorry is a large goods vehicle, a truck
provided means on condition that
R is short for regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: Applause for a splendid royal vehicle laid on for the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The second R of the vehicle word gives way to IF. A lorry is the British word for a truck.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: exalting someone with lavish acclaim and honour, as in hymns to God, is commending them highly.

clue.text: Heavenly body in tight leotards

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: An admirer praises a gorgeous figure in figure-hugging leotards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly body' reads as a compliment to a dancer; it means a star.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodestar is a guiding star, especially the Pole Star used in navigation, so it is a celestial object.

clue.text: Obstruction blocking path — this is for the better

indicators.note: something blocking a path stands in the middle of it, so it goes inside

blocks.note: a route is a path or way
let is an old word for hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A barrier across the footpath is said to be an improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like 'improved'; read it as one who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: Roulette is a casino game played for gamblers' stakes, so it exists for the bettor.

clue.text: Stirring up succeeded, as far as leader’s concerned

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees
to means up to, as far as
a king is a ruler or leader

explanation.surface: Someone stirs up trouble successfully, at least in the leader's eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoking a fire means poking and feeding it, and figuratively stoking means inciting or stirring up feelings.

clue.text: Fresh waters off the south coast here

blocks.note: here means in, as in at home
the Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and the English south coast

explanation.surface: Clean, fresh seawater is found here along the southern shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' looks like clean water; it means cheeky. The words come in reverse order: here, then the waters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh in the sense of cheeky or impertinent matches insolent, meaning rudely disrespectful.

clue.text: Bar reduced expenditure on whiskey

indicators.note: reduced means cut down, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: outlay is money spent
Whiskey is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for W

explanation.surface: A pub has cut back its spending on whiskey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub; it is the verb meaning to forbid.
explanation.definitionFit: To outlaw something is to ban or prohibit it, which is what barring means.

clue.text: Gucci to review turning clothes blue

indicators.note: clothes as a verb means covers or dresses, so the answer is wrapped inside the words
turning means facing the other way, so the hidden letters read backwards

blocks.note: the letters running across the end of Gucci, all of to, and the start of review

explanation.surface: Gucci must reconsider its racy line of blue garments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' and 'blue' suggest fashion colours, yet clothes is a verb and blue means risqué.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue films or jokes are sexually explicit, which is what erotic describes.

clue.text: Poor artist content to leave drama company giving people a lift

indicators.note: when the content leaves, only the shell remains, so just the outside letters stay

blocks.note: the first and last letters of drama
Uber is the ride-hailing firm

explanation.surface: A struggling artist happily quits a theatre troupe to drive for a ride-hailing firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like 'happy'; it means the insides of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A dauber smears paint about crudely, so the word describes an unskilled painter.

clue.text: Disregarding the odds, goalie’s giving encouragement

indicators.note: disregarding the odd positions leaves only the even ones, the second, fourth and sixth letters

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of goalie

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper defies the odds and lifts the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The odds' sounds like betting chances, but it means the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Olé is the Spanish cheer shouted at bullfights and football matches to urge players on.

clue.text: Pole stole hot pants, given fine

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the word beside it is badly arranged

blocks.note: a boa is a long feathery scarf, a kind of stole
the letters of hot rearranged
OK means fine, all right

explanation.surface: A Pole steals some sexy shorts and is fined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person and 'stole' like theft; both are objects. 'Pants' is British slang for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A boathook is a long pole with a hook used to push off or pull in a boat.

clue.text: Cursing son short of energy

blocks.note: S is short for son
someone weary is tired, low on energy

explanation.surface: A worn-out son starts swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short of' looks like a deletion signal; the whole phrase simply means tired.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweary is informal for full of swear words, which describes cursing speech.

clue.text: Perhaps one’s given order to steam trains?

definitions.text: Perhaps one’s given order to steam trains?

indicators.note: putting something in order means arranging it afresh, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A railway official awaits instructions to get the old steam locomotives running.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: a railway official might well be told to get the steam trains running.
explanation.definitionFit: A stationmaster runs a railway station and could plausibly be instructed to send the steam locomotives on their way.
